newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries sharply up, Fed hike doubts emerge.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries sharply up, Fed hike doubts emerge.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities ended sharply higher on Friday after surprisingly subdued consumer inflation and retail sales reports cast doubt on prospects for a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike later this month, economists said.
The market began actively questioning the inevitability of a rate rise on Thursday, after the Labor Department reported a drop in August core producer prices.
Friday's numbers only reinforced the potential for steady policy and sent prices soaring in early high-volume dealings.
"The data today lent credibiltiy to the argument that the Fed can wait -- that there's not a compelling reason for them to move in September," said Mitchell Held, chief economist at Smith Barney Inc.

The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond ended up 1-15/32 at 97-14/32 to yield 6.95 percent, the lowest closing yield in approximately three weeks. The 6.125 percent two-year note ended up 9/32 at 100-00/32 to yield 6.12 percent.

The Labor Department reported on Friday that consumer prices rose a paltry 0.1 percent in both overall and core readings during the month of August compared to 0.3 percent gains in both figures last month. Economists surveyed by Reuters had been calling for a 0.2 percent gain across the board.

More importantly, retail sales for the month of August came in signficantly below market expectations, rising only 0.2 percent in both headline and ex-autos readings. Consensus forecasts had called for a 0.7 percent overall rise and a 0.4 percent gain excluding automobiles.
Treasuries surged in the immediate aftermath of the numbers -- particularly in the one to two-year sector -- reflecting a widespread reassessment of tightening prospects.
But while economists admitted that odds for a rate hike had diminished, many were sticking to their guns and predicting tighter credit come September 24.

"I know a lot of people have swung back to steady policy (forecasts), but I think the chances are still slightly better than 50 percent that they will make a move and dress it up as if it's just taking back the January ease," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.

Stiles said comments from Federal Reserve Governor Lawrence Lindsey, which took the market off its highs in afternoon trade, suggested that even "doves" on the Federal Open Market Committee, are highly concerned about an uptick in inflation.

Lindsey told Reuters on Friday that Fed policy was "a tad on the low side" of neutral. He also told Bridge News that the election campaign would not prevent the Fed from moving and that things could get "out of hand" if the Fed did not move.

In other economic news, the University of Michigan's preliminary index of consumer sentiment for September fell to 95.0 from 95.3 in the final August index, but analysts said the report had little market impact.
Three-month bill rates closed off six basis points at 5.07 percent, six-month bill rates were off eight basis points at 5.18 percent and year-bill rates fell 13 basis points to 5.44 percent.
The Treasury's 6.5 percent five-year note climbed 22/32 to 100-03/32 to yield 6.48 percent and its 7.0 percent 10-year note rose 1-2/32 to 101-30/32, yielding 6.73 percent.
